episode.showDescription: Cougar Sports with Ben Criddle (@criddlebenjamin) keeps you up-to-date on all things BYU Sports. We not only cover football & basketball, but we dive into recruiting, baseball, soccer, and more. For insight that you can't get anywhere else, tune into 103.9/ 98.3 FM. Monday-Friday from 2-6 PM MST. Follow us on social media @espnthefan & interact with us using #ESPNTheFan.

transcript_window.text: Where do we stand?
Well, it's a big question, obviously.
I think the great thing about college football is it remains the second most popular sport in this country behind the NFL.
So despite all of the friction and all the issues that the sport is facing, it's still immensely popular.
and even all the negativity around it has not impacted that in a really, really meaningful way yet.
I think that we have, the powers that be have just got to understand that we have something so unique in this game.

And you may, all of us who have been around college football for our entire careers, know that there is something in the DNA of this sport that literally makes it different than anything else in the world, and so those of us who are on the ground have to keep executing and doing what makes the sport special and

at the same time we hope that the conference commissioners and the management committee and even congress as they're getting involved understand that we need to preserve what makes it special otherwise we just become you know nfl part two yeah and there are many people that want that there are some that want it within the college
football landscape to become become the NFL part two, but there's got to be something more.
There's something more intrinsic and valuable with the, the logos, the universities, the, the alumni that are a part of these these college football organizations.

And you know, you've been a part of this journey for a long time is, as you look at the movements, right, where people want to go within the sport, what are the biggest frictions that we're dealing with right now?
And I look at frictions as opportunities, by the way, Look at these frictional moments.
There are opportunities for growth.
There opportunities to probably have a better product on the football field, better entertainment, better storylines, et cetera.
But what do you see on the horizon?
Yeah, I 100 % agree.
My philosophy is that obstacles are opportunities, and you have to live that way.
And I think if we approach the game that way, it's going to be hard to kill college football.
Not that it can't be done, but if we don't make the right corrections at this point, it had risks going in that direction.
I think the ultimate friction point is with the student athletes, what rights they have, both legally and from a financial opportunity standpoint, mitigating and figuring out where those stand.
Because obviously the pendulum has really swung from one end of the spectrum where the student athletes had few rights and no opportunity, and we're at the far other end of the spectrum.

tough to swing back to the middle but that's the battle right now i think that that's the key and they're trying to address it in this protect college sports act and everybody else trying to work behind the scenes and build coalitions ultimately we need to figure out how we can make sure the players are represented fairly they
have an opportunity through nil or what other mechanisms they put in place to be compensated fairly but at the same time we protect the integrity of the sport.
So you don't have a young man who plays for five teams in five years.
And it doesn't build a legacy, doesn't build any sort of community, doesn't build.
I mean, they're transacting wherever they go in this ultimate free agent market, but they're not really building anything that that's enduring.
